Psychiatry and Foreign Affairs: A Vision and a Commitment

William Davidson MD

William Davidson

P.O. Box 7630
Falls Church, VA 22046.

William Davidson  

The central vision of psychiatry is transformation. Psychiatrists, and most certainly psychoanalysts, assume that their patients can transcend the historical genesis of their pain, conflicts, and delusions.

It was Einstein who first clearly articulated the possibility that this fundamental vision of psychiatry might also be of service to the increasingly destructive situation among the nation-states of the world. In his now famous correspondence with Freud he asked Freud whether it was possible to guide the psychological development of man so that it becomes resistant to the psychoses of hate and destruction. This possibility has fascinated and challenged a small but enthusiastic group ever since.

Psychiatrists have undergone a continuing expansion of their interests and competence. They have moved from an initial concern with intrapsychic, interpersonal, and intrafamilial conflict to the broader areas of conflict in the community and conflict between social and racial groups. This paper presents a vision of psychiatry in a world context and describes the 18-year commitment of one psychiatrist to make that vision a reality.

Dr. Davidson is the President and founder of the Institute for Psychiatry and Foreign Affairs, Washington, D.C. Formerly, he was Research Psychiatrist, Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, U.S. Department of State; Research Fellow, Department of Social Relations, Harvard University; and Fellow, Community Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital.

Helen Gediman PHD

Helen Gediman

40 East 89th Street, $14D
New York, N.Y. 10128

Helen Gediman  

Psychoanalytic institutes are sometimes more or less “taken in” by candidates who suffer from imposturous tendencies of one degree or other. Supervisors, evaluators, Progression Committee members may constitute, for the candidate with imposturous tendencies, the “audience” that inadvertently heightens imposturous ego trends. Supervisors may unwittingly reinforce a candidate's “false self” because they are susceptible, as are we all, to identifying unconsciously with the wished-for omnipotence that the imposturous candidate expresses so obviously and ego-syntonically (see Gediman, 1985). What has been identified, often after a long-delayed recognition, as a form of pathological imposture may indeed resemble, phenomenologically, the first steps of the normal process of learning to become a psychoanalyst. In the beginning, we are not surprised if we observe a certain degree of unintegrated role-playing. In addition, the neophyte trainee is encouraged to assume, in a controlled and limited sense, multiple identifications with both patients and supervisors in order to develop empathy and analytic wisdom.

Helen K. Gediman, Ph.D., is Clinical Professor of Psychology, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy; Faculty, New York Freudian Society.

The Transformation of Thought That the Nuclear Age Requires: Can We Achieve It?

Robert Wallerstein MD

Robert Wallerstein

401 Parnassus Avenue, Box 40C
San Francisco, CA 94143.

Robert Wallerstein  

Psychoanalytic discourse on the problems of aggression and war usually takes its point of departure from the famous exchange of letters between Einstein and Freud, “Why War?” (Freud, 1933), although that exchange is now more than half a century old and occurred before the advent of the nuclear age when the question of war was not yet that of the very survival of the human species on a livable planet. In that interchange, Einstein interspersed a number of assertions about human psychology with questions addressed to Freud. He asked, “How is it these devices succeed so well in rousing men to such wild enthusiasm, even to sacrifice their lives? Only one answer is possible. Because man has within him a lust for hatred and destruction…. And so we come to our last question. Is it possible to control man's mental evolution so as to make him proof against the psychoses of hate and destructiveness?” (p. 201; italics added). Certainly a serious question for one of the world's intellectual giants to address to the creator of psychoanalysis who had done so much to illuminate the dark side of man's instinctual life.

Freud's answer to these queries began modestly and almost apologetically.

Dr. Wallerstein is Professor at the Department of Psychiatry, University of California, San Francisco.

Kohut's Testament

Lawrence Friedman MD

Lawrence Friedman

129 B East 71st Street
New York, NY 10021

Lawrence Friedman  

An analytic theoretician can leave us no richer legacy than a forthright statement of his theory of cure. How Does Analysis Cure? is just such a testament: concise, unflinching, and frank about the atmospheric realities that are often primly left to gossip. Kohut has lined up his teachings in bright sunlight for any contest, disdaining to make them seem all things to all men. And since Kohut was primarily interested in treatment rather than systems, every practitioner will recognize his reasons, and will find a fresh chance to examine the ultimate question in the title.

Additionally, by responding to various understandings and misunderstandings, Kohut lets us have another go at self psychology, and another chance to place it in relation to current Freudian theory. Although this book presumes familiarity with Kohut's theory of the mind, it may be the best introduction just because it is not encumbered with schematic detail, and because it proceeds by informal discussion of treatment.

Pathogenesis

Kohut's well-known belief is that psychological illness is an aborted effort to build a coherent structure of usable ambitions and ideals.

Dr. Friedman is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and Member of the Section on the History of Psychiatry, New York Hospital, Cornell University Medical Center.

The Domestic Rationale for Foreign Enemies

Paul Warnke ESQ

Paul Warnke

815 Connecticut Avenue
Washington, DC 20006

Paul Warnke  

Dr. Pinderhughes' paper raises for me the question whether nations need enemies. Is it somehow essential to their national identity? As Dr. Mack has pointed out, in a war, of course, we tend to dehumanize the enemy. It makes it easier to kill them and easier to run the risk of being killed yourself. Even in peacetime, you may remember that Senator Vandenburg told President Truman that he could not get the Marshall Plan through Congress unless he built up the Red menace. So there is always this incentive to find an outside enemy. And, of course, one is very handy when you are trying to get through a several-billion-dollar defense budget. In the absence of a bogey man the budget might have far tougher sledding.

Our problem today is that we are running out of acceptable enemies. At one point we could count on Red China, and Dean Rusk could talk about the specter of a billion Chinese armed with nuclear weapons. Today we have a billion Chinese and they are armed with nuclear weapons, but they scare nobody but the Russians. Similarly, we have the task of trying to rationalize the use of force in our foreign policy. We have to find a foe worthy of our steel. Clearly it was not Vietnam, nor was it Grenada. It is not Nicaragua. We have to find a worthy enemy. So the entire burden has now fallen on the Soviets. I do not know what we would do without them.

Mr. Warnke is a practicing attorney in Washington, D.C. and Chairman of the Committee for National Security.

Carl Nedelmann MD

Carl Nedelmann

Averhoffstr. 7
D-2000 Hamburg 76
West Germany

Carl Nedelmann  

If you make yourself an advocate of reason, be prepared to be branded a communist. Sadly, that is as far as the enemies of tolerance and humanity are able to think.

— Albert Schweitzer, 1961

In November of 1983 the parliament of the German Federal Republic, despite widespread and articulate opposition from the peace movement, agreed to the deployment of the Pershing-II missiles on German soil. The missile decision means that, for the first time in postwar history, the German Federal Republic agreed to deploy weapons that can reach the Russian power centers in and around Moscow. The different interpretations of the military nature of these weapons are important. The Russians consider the Pershing II “strategic” weapons comparable to intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Western nations consider them “tactical” weapons comparable to other weapons in the “nuclear theatre”, which means Europe. This different assessment is serious. It is more than merely a propaganda game between the superpowers. It affects West German relations with both the United States and the Soviet Union.

Dr. Nedelmann is Director of the Michael Balint Institute, Hamburg.

The German version of this essay, written in 1984, was translated by Claude Wedeles in cooperation with the author.

Epilogue

Ernest Wolf Issue Editor

Ernest Wolf

Ernest Wolf  

In nature's infinite book of secrecy, A little I can read.

— Anthony and Cleopatra

Ashort 20 years ago Heinz Kohut burst upon the psychoanalytic world with his essay “Forms and Transformations of Narcissism,” heralding a new psychology of the self. To be sure, the discerning observer can in retrospect detect the seeds for the new ideas in his 1959 article “Introspection, Empathy, and Psychoanalysis,” which was aptly subtitled “An Examination of the Relationship Between Mode of Observation and Theory.” Indeed, as Goldberg reminds us, this latter article contained enough controversial ideas about empathy and psychoanalytic science to have almost been rejected by the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association, and it was the vigorous intervention of Maxwell Gitelson that prevailed over the timid souls who were clinging to obsolete aspects of an honorable tradition. Thus was forecast the fate of Kohutian self psychology: to repeat within the smaller circle of the psychoanalytic community the history that Freudian psychoanalysis had experienced — and is experiencing — within the wider circle of medical psychology. To paraphrase Goldberg, the history of psychoanalysis is replete with attempts to solve scientific controversy by administrative fiat. Though occasionally successful in exiling pioneering thinkers — Adler, Rank, and Horney come to mind most prominently, but there were others — suppression of many of their most creative ideas have never been equally successful but have regularly been absorbed into the mainstream, albeit without appropriate attribution to their originators.

The Influence of Psychogeography Upon the Conduct of International Relations: Clinical and Metapsychological Considerations

Howard Stein PHD

Howard Stein

P. O. Box 26901
Oklahoma City, OK 73190

Howard Stein  

This essay approaches intergroup, specifically international, relations from the perspective of psychogeography. I argue that a psychogeographic understanding of people's perception and investment in their own group and in other groups, and of consequent actions, contributes a needed dimension toward understanding the nature of international conflict. Although a plethora of studies of national character, ethnicity, and group identity have been written since the 1930s, little has been said of the relation between one's sense of group identity and sense of place. Psychogeography, the psychoanalytic study of spatial representation (Stein, 1984c; see also Niederland, 1956, 1957, 1971a, 1971b; Volkan, 1979) is an approach that may help to unravel why who one is comes to be experienced as indistinguishable from where one is, and in turn where and who others are perceived to be in relation to one.

In its widest compass, psychogeography consists of the representation of developmental time and the playing out of its vicissitudes on the stage of space.

Dr. Stein is Professor, Department of Family Medicine, University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center; and Editor of The Journal of Psychoanalytic Anthropology.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein, Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein,

Melvin Bornstein,  

Our pioneering effort to bring the concept of power into the mainstream of psychoanalytic inquiry has led to contributions diverse in subject and formulation. Nonetheless, when the papers are viewed as a whole, a predominant theme emerges: current psychoanalytic reliance on theories of aggression and sadism, on anxiety and defense, are inadequate to deal with the causality and phenomenology of power. A psychoanalytic study of power requires a comprehensive consideration of ego functions (Loewenberg), deficits in self and ego regulation (Grotstein and Person), interaction (Gediman), and the consolidation of sexual identity (Adams-Silvan and Silvan). In an earlier issue Meissner (1985) stated that, despite criticisms and proposed alternatives, traditional metapsychology offers the greatest promise for the assimilation of complete intrapsychic and interactional viewpoints. Detailed analytic study of concepts like power that bridge these points of view provide a challenging test for Meissner's hypothesis.

Epilogue

John Mack Issue Editor

John Mack

John Mack  

Long before the nuclear superpowers began to extend their competition into space Bertrand Russell (1959) wrote, “When I read of plans to defile the heavens by the petty squabbles of the animated lumps that disgrace a certain planet, I cannot but feel that the men who make these plans are guilty of a kind of impiety” (p. 19). Russell's words lead us to a central dynamic, the arrogance of power of nations spiritually adrift, terrorized by the destructive energy that their scientists have released from particles of matter.

The self-glorification of nations lies at the root of war, the conviction that “it is right to pursue the interests of one's own nation however they may conflict with those of others” (Russell, p. 78). The proclamation of superiority and special rights, interests, and virtues is tolerated, even applauded, when put forth by the leaders and citizens of national collectivities, whereas such behaviors or attitudes would be regarded as unacceptable if expressed by individuals.

Aggression in our technologically sophisticated age takes bizarre, remote forms. It is difficult to find the locus of responsibility for it among advanced systems of computers, strange weaponry, distant institutions, sanitized language and elaborate justifications. But it is diffusely present nevertheless, complexly organized in our war institutions, multinational corporate structures, and related collective organizations. It comes to the surface more readily when national and subnational groups experience real or imagined injuries to their collective egoism.

Freud and those who have followed him, working with individual patients, have identified the unconscious psychological forces that limit the possibilities of human well-being and fulfillment.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

John Mack Issue Editor

John Mack

John Mack  

Aglance at the morning newspapers or television news broadcasts is all we need to be convinced that the darkest, most destructive elements in human nature are given continuous expression in the conduct of international relations. War, and other forms of mass killing in the service of a political cause, mounting on occasion to the level of genocide, are the regular stuff of contemporary international political life. Some of this violence, or the threat of it, may, from an ethnic or national group's standpoint, be justified on the basis of more or less well-defined purposes or “interests.” But other killing seems little more than the naked expression of hatred and aggression, usually as part of a cycle of vengeance or retaliation for previously experienced victimization.

The nuclear-weapons competition, led by the United States and the Soviet Union, has done a great deal to focus the attention of students of international relations upon the dark, irrational dimensions of human nature, that domain of human psychological life which psychoanalysts have been exploring for nearly a century. The purposeful development of weapons so destructive that their possessors are deterred from using them out of fear of unacceptable retribution is not itself irrational. But the world has witnessed something more than simple deterrence. The United States and the Soviet Union have tried to use nuclear weapons for purposes of political coercion and dominance (Kincade, 1985). They and the other nuclear powers have developed weapon systems ever more technologically sophisticated, as if real advantage could be gained, wars won, or countries defended through the use of nuclear devices.

Dr. Mack is Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School, The Cambridge Hospital.

Dealing with Conflict among Individuals and Nations: Are There Common Principles?

Roger Fisher L.L.B.

Roger Fisher

Pound Hall 524
Harvard Law School
1563 Massachusetts Avenue
Cambridge, MA 02138

Roger Fisher  

Why war? Are there common principles that apply both to conflict among individuals and to conflict among nations? It seems obvious that the answer is yes, since in both cases it is people that are involved, human beings like you and me. But before we can deal with a problem we need to clarify what the problem is. Let me submit that the problem is not conflict.

Many people assume that our goal is to resolve all our conflicts, to wake up one morning with our conflicts resolved so we can then have peace. Clearly, that is unrealistic. We will have more conflicts next year than we had last. As I say to students who wonder whether they are going into a promising area of study, “conflict is a growth industry.” One hundred years ago, we and Canada had a dispute over the precise location of a granite boundary marker on the Minnesota line. Today, it is over acid rain. The difference in complexity, the difference in numbers of people involved, and the difference in the financial, economic, and social consequences is typical. Every day, internationally as well as domestically, we have more interactions and more cause for conflict. With technological progress, conflict comes more rapidly and more people want to have a say about what happens.

Mr. Fisher is a Professor at Harvard Law School.

Peter Loewenberg PHD

Peter Loewenberg

Los Angeles, California 90024

Peter Loewenberg  

Freud initiated the enterprise we now call psychohistory not merely because he was a curious commentator, critic, and analyst of civilization who wished to present a “general psychology” that was valid for all mankind, and not merely because he was a deeply cultured man who would have preferred to be a philosopher rather than a clinician. He committed his psychodynamic ideas to the problems of history, culture, art, and literary criticism also as a strategy of presentation to circumvent the evidential problem of case histories. No one fully knows what goes on in any clinical psychoanalytic setting. Even in the Rat Man Case where we have Freud's notes, there is much that we must infer and will never know. Freud chose to demonstrate his insights and formulae of mental functioning by reference to the works of Leonardo and Michelangelo, Shakespeare, and Ibsen because these data and artifacts belong to the culture at large. Any person may obtain, study, scrutinize, and question Freud's interpretations from the same data base to see if they make sense or convey conviction. In their persistent quest for a more accurate model of the mind, Freud and his successors created models that reflected shifts in the culture at large; thus, the recent interest in narcissism.

Professor Loewenberg is a Professor of History, University of California, Los Angeles; member of the Faculty of the Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute. He is author of Decoding the Past: The Psychohistorical Approach (1985) and is an editor of the Psychohistory Review.

The Power of the Wish and the Wish for Power: A Discussion of Power and Psychoanalysis

Bennett Simon MD

Bennett Simon

170 Chestnut Street
West Newton, MA. 02165

Bennett Simon  

We are presented here with five papers solicited for and submitted for an issue of this journal on the subject of power. The papers, each interesting and valuable in its own right, add up to only a patchwork of contributions to a psychoanalytic overview of power. This discussion, then, will take up primarily the various dimensions of the problem(s) of power and psychoanalysis, and secondarily show the place that these particular papers occupy on that dimensional map.

In order for psychoanalysts to have credibility in discussing power it is crucial to examine why and how psychoanalysts (and psychoanalysis) are interested in power. What is the relationship between psychoanalysis and power? What is the power or the kinds of power we eschew, and for what kinds of power do we yearn but rarely achieve?

Let us consider who writes about power? Like many other important things in life, those who have plenty and the assurance of plenty of some commodity tend not to think too much about that commodity, let alone analyze and write it. Lack, not plenty, motivates inquiry.

Bennett Simon, M.D., is Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School (Beth Israel Hospital); Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Hartmann's hopes for psychoanalysis becoming a general psychology and achieving the status of a natural science have not been realized. Today there are numerous models available to explain a variety of psychological data, some better suited than psychoanalysis. Furthermore, the place of psychoanalysis in either natural science or social science remains the subject of debate. Edelson states that psychoanalysis cannot explain everything that is psychological. Meissner, Smith, and Greenberg believe that at our current state of knowledge psychoanalysis is deficient as a comprehensive psychological theory. We believe that they are conveying a message — the message that there remain unexplored bridges within the body of Hartmann's work that will strengthen the explanatory power of metapsychology and classical psychoanalysis in the areas of experience, self psychology, and object relations. The structural theory and metapsychology remain as an essential starting point for developing any comprehensive understanding of the workings of the mind.

A Diplomat among Psychoanalysts

Joseph Moniville A.M.

Joseph Moniville

3749 Yorktown Village Pass
Annandale, VA 22003

Joseph Moniville  

In this short paper, I try to explain how an American career diplomat discovered the critical importance of psychoanalytic theory to political analysis and the making of foreign policy. This is a daunting task, not least because I have never formally studied psychoanalysis, and my knowledge of its extensive literature is limited. But perhaps there is an advantage in this.

Whenever I came across a theory that explained a political, especially conflicted, situation to me, I made a note of it and continued on about my professional business. I was lucky enough to meet several psychoanalysts and psychoanalytically sensitive psychiatrists and political psychologists in Washington in the 1970s. And after a few years, I was able to write (in collaboration with William D. Davidson) (Davidson and Montville, 1981) an article entitled “Foreign Policy According to Freud,” which was published in the prestigious quarterly, Foreign Policy. This was my first major attempt to marry psychological theory and real-world problems and the beginning of a theory-building process that had started some 15 years earlier.

My first foreign service post was Baghdad, Iraq, in 1965. The basic lesson for a political officer there was that real political identities in Iraq—and therefore loyalties—were found in substate or subnational groupings.

Mr. Montville is Research Director, Center for the Study of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Service Institute, Department of State.

In the early 1930s, the billboards of England carried advertisements for paint in which white-coated workmen spelled out the brand name by painting its successive letters on the backs of the men in front of them. Dualism Revisited: Schafer, Hartmann, and Freud

Joseph Smith MD

Joseph Smith

4705 Locust Hill Court
Bethesda, MD 20814

Joseph Smith  

Just as Roy Schafer's “An Overview of Heinz Hartmann's Contributions to Psychoanalysis” (1970) was half about Hartmann, half about Schafer, and all about Freud, I write half about Hartmann, half about Freud, and all about Schafer. I shall “defend” (defend in quotes because it is largely a negative defense) Hartmann against compliments in Schafer's overview that he would not have wanted, e.g., that he cracked the dualistic framework of Freudian thought, and against criticisms that he did not deserve, e.g., that his work was flawed by allegiance to a natural science approach.

The overview rhetorical strategies I question are:

The implicit assumption that psychic energy, postulated for explanatory purposes (i.e., with qualities), metapsychology, the biological vantage, the natural science approach, and psychoanalysis being (or having prospects of becoming) a general psychology all stand or fall together. Arguments against one should count against the others.

The implicit assumption that arguments against simplistic dualisms or the simplistic deployment of dualisms count against any dualistic thinking.

Joseph H. Smith, M.D. is Supervising and Training Analyst, The Washington Psychoanalytic Institute; Co-Editor, Psychiatry and the Humanities; and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences.

Non Omnis Moriar

Arnold Goldberg MD

Arnold Goldberg

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, IL 60601

Arnold Goldberg  

Sometime in the 1970s Heinz Kohut gave up his teaching tasks at the Institute for Psychoanalysis and asked me to take over his class on self psychology. I remember that first class meeting very well because I felt very enthusiastic about the job, and I facetiously began by announcing that I was not Heinz Kohut. To my surprise and dismay one person got up and walked out. Although I later learned that the man actually was registered for another course, I have always recalled that moment whenever I have assumed the stand-in posture for my mentor. Over the years I have frequently navigated my way between what Kohut would say and what I might say, but my response to these reviews and critiques of this last book of his will clearly call for my trying to speak for Heinz Kohut. Actually this is not such a difficult job for me not only because it was a frequent request from Heinz as well as from others, but also because all of us who were associated with self psychology have felt very strongly that it must not be an orthodoxy and cannot be judged as the work of one man. Over the years there have been so many discussions about the work with such a plethora of exchanges of ideas, that I feel fairly sure that after Kohut's first book every succeeding publication contained ideas gathered from us all. Kohut was the originator and developer of self psychology, but he wanted nothing more than to see it continue to grow and develop on its own and ultimately without him.

Dr. Goldberg is Clinical Professor, Rush Medical School, and Training and Supervising Analyst, Institute for Psychoanalysis, Chicago.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

For over a quarter of a century Heinz Hartmann's writings dominated psychoanalysis in the United States. Beginning with Ego Psychology and the Problem of Adaptation (1939), Hartmann set out to refine the incomplete structural theory left by Freud, to lead psychoanalysis toward becoming a general psychology, and to guarantee a place for psychoanalysis in the realm of natural science. In Ego Psychology and the Problem of Adaptation, Hartmann outlined the framework and the raw structure of his ideas, which he elaborated, refined, and explored in numerous essays during the next 30 years.

It is still premature for a determination of how successful Hartmann has been. However, we believe that it is impossible to understand psychoanalysis as a clinical and theoretical discipline without an appreciation of his work. A brief summary of the content of his contributions follows.

In a detailed study of the ego Hartmann described the ego as comprised of multiple substructures and subfunctions with primary and secondary autonomy, some conflict-free, others capable of shifting from conflict-free to conflicted areas of activity. With the ego's multiple foci of activity he established that human action was not the result of drives and defense but of a spectrum of apparatuses which reflect defenses, cognition, and automation. By defining adaptation as a biological process characteristic of all living things, he was able to place the data of psychoanalysis within the realm of natural science.

Furthermore, upon establishing the multiple foci of ego activity relative to drives and adaptation and differentiating between self, ego, and self-representation, he opened the exploration for an object relations theory.

Heinz Hartmann's Influence on Psychoanalysis as a Science

Marshall Edelson M.D., Ph.D.

Marshall Edelson

25 Park Street — GB 617
New Haven, CT 06519

Marshall Edelson  

The work of heinz hartmann was motivated, in part at least, by his wish to contribute to achieving one primary objective. He thought psychoanalysis should be a general psychology, and his theoretical essays addressed the problem of making it one. In this paper, I do not attempt to explicate or assess what and how much that was valuable he added to psychoanalytic theory as he went about this task. Schafer (1970) has already described and evaluated these additions. I do want, however, to consider the consequences for the development of psychoanalysis as a science of pursuing this objective.

In short, I argue that adopting such an objective obscures just which domain of phenomena psychoanalysis is most likely to be able to explain. Furthermore, psychoanalysis may pursue this objective by imperialistically incorporating the knowledge of other disciplines — often merely translating their terminology into that of psychoanalysis — but the price of this “enrichment” is that psychoanalytic theory becomes increasingly unwieldy and difficult to test.

Dr. Edelson is Professor of Psychiatry, Yale University; Director of Research in the Outpatient Division of Yale's Connecticut Mental Health Center; and a Member of the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Portions of this paper have appeared elsewhere in a somewhat different form (see Edelson, 1986a, b).

The Relationship of Psychosexual Development to the Successful Exercise of Power in a Woman Ruler: A Study of Catherine dé Medici

Abby Adams-Silvan PHD and Mark Silvan PHD

Mark Silvan

300 Central Park West
New York, N. Y. 10024

Mark Silvan  

This study of Catherine dé Medici is descriptive rather than explanatory, an informed speculation regarding the dynamics and character of one whose history—not presence—is available to us. Although we lack details about Catherine's inner experience, we do have the scope of her entire life on which to base our ideas. From the accomplishments and failures of historical figures in their public and private lives, we can hope to identify salient strengths, deficits, flaws, and patterns (Stein, 1977).

This paper is part of a longer study of three queens—Mary, Queen of Scots, Elizabeth I, and Catherine dé Medici—who were pivotal in the political maelstrom of sixteenth-century Europe. Because these women wielded great power, their accomplishments—or the lack thereof—were glaringly reflected in the magnifying mirror of national events.

Abby Adams-Silvan is Associate Clinical Professor, New York University Post-Doctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy; Member and Faculty, New York Freudian Society and Psychoanalytic Training Institute.

Charles Pinderhughes  

Freud and Einstein on War

Albert Einstein and Sigmund Freud the 20th century's best-known scientists, had a common interest in the causes of war and the promotion of peace. Einstein was a consummate pacifist. As a boy he was repelled by militarism, bigotry, authoritarianism, and nationalism, and as a man he struggled to comprehend how people who are thoroughly decent in personal conduct with associates can show such utterly antithetical behavior with others (Nathan & Norden, 1980).

Yet even this gentle man could not advocate pacifism vis-à-vis Nazism in Germany. Although apprehensive about the potential for abuse of any concentration of power, he recommended to President Roosevelt in 1939 that the United States support work to develop an atomic bomb. He did this, not with the idea that the United States would use it, but so that the United States, having it, could deter a Germany he feared soon would have it.

In 1931 Einstein invited Freud to join an association of intellectuals to exercise moral and political influence and to provide moral support for international agencies like the League of Nations.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Lawrence Friedman concludes his commentary by stating, “No reservation will diminish Kohut's gigantic clinical contribution. Regardless of theory, the problem of treatment is to hook up with the patient's trying, and to make it profitable in one way or another. Laurels go to the man who gives us new ways to visualize what a patient is trying for. And that Kohut has surely done.”

Kohut's, How Does Analysis Cure? (1984), published posthumously, edited by Arnold Goldberg with the collaboration of Paul E. Stepansky and assistance of Elizabeth Kohut, represents Kohut's final extended thoughts on the analytic process. The book contains the clearest statement of a lifetime effort to explore how analysis works. Regardless of whether the reader accepts the premises of self psychology and of self and selfobject and its reformulations of empathy transmutation and internalization, the issues these concepts bring into focus are invaluable to all psychoanalytic clinicians and theoreticians. Our commentators differ as to the weight to be given to the Kohutian perspective, reflecting the diversity of views present in the analytic community.

Kohut devotes the first section of How Does Analysis Cure? to clarifications and responses to criticisms of his last book, Restoration of the Self. He presents his most current view of psychic development and pathogenesis. Emphasizing the experience-near perspective, Kohut places fragmentation anxiety of the self as the fundamental anxiety of human existence. Fragmentation anxiety is the result of failure of selfobjects to provide the self with solidity, harmony, and the impetus for maturation. Maturation leads to the capacity to utilize mature selfobjects throughout life.

The Self in Psychoanalysis and in Phenomenological Philosophy

Paul Ricoeur PHD

Paul Ricoeur

1025 East 58th Street
Chicago, IL 60637

Paul Ricoeur  

My contribution to the study of the last—and alas posthumous—work of Heinz Kohut, How Does Analysis Cure? (1984), does not have the ambition of arbitrating the quarrel among psychoanalytic schools concerning the respective places of such concepts as “consciousness,” “ego,” and “self.” Instead, by accepting as a quite plausible working hypothesis the metapsychology of self psychology and the analytic technique corresponding to it, I would like to reflect upon their import for philosophical reflection concerned with the relationships between subjectivity and intersubjectivity. Hence I will assume the same attitude that I held when I was writing Freud and Philosophy (1970), namely, to let myself be instructed by analytic experience in order to learn what it can teach us about what philosophical reflection cannot draw from its own grounds.

In the first part of this essay I present a summary of the themes that will figure in the confrontation with philosophy that will take place in the second part.

The Major Themes of the Metapsychology of Self

It is first of all important to obtain an exact measurement of the gap between Kohut's metapsychology and what he calls “traditional analysis,” namely, that of Freud, as prolonged by ego analysis.

Paul Ricoeur, Ph.D., is John Nuveen Professor Emeritus, University of Chicago.

James Grotstein MD

James Grotstein

9777 Wilshire Boulevard
Beverly Hills, CA 90212

James Grotstein  

When we attempt to understand psychopathology, we are confronted by two separate traditions or approaches, that of psychoanalysis and that of empirical psychiatry. The basic assumptions of the former derive from the considerations of the vicissitudes of drives, manifested in a dynamic matrix of psychical conflict between those drives and nurturing objects that become enmeshed with them. The traditional psychoanalytic conception of psychopathology seems based, consequently, on a theory of power. Empirical psychiatry, on the other hand, offers pathological conceptions which implicate defects or deficiencies in psychical functioning, some of which may be inherited, others of which may develop in infancy and childhood. More recent contributions to psychoanalysis have complicated the seeming simplicity of this duality by suggesting a developmental deficit concept of psychic structure harkening back to Freud's (1911) concept of decathexis.

Dr. Grotstein is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at UCLA, Attending Staff Physician at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and Director of the Interdisciplinary Group for Advanced Studies in Primitive Mental States. This contribution is offered under the auspices of the latter.

Critical Reflections on the Theory of Self Psychology: An Inside View

Robert Stolorow PHD

Robert Stolorow

Suite 410
11726 San Vicente Boulevard
Los Angeles, CA 90049

Robert Stolorow  

In the opening paragraph of his book, Kohut (1984) characterized How Does Analysis Cure? as an effort to clarify and further elaborate ideas that he had set forth earlier in The Restoration of the Self (1977). His final book may be read as a kind of “progress report” on the current status of a new theoretical system still in an early phase of intensive development. It is this evolving framework that is the focus of my essay.

Introduction

Since the publication of The Restoration of the Self, in which Kohut firmly demarcated his theoretical system from that of classical metapsychology, the psychoanalytic literature has abounded in critical reactions to self psychology from its opponents and, less frequently, rejoinders to these criticisms by its advocates. The present paper is, I believe, unique in that it offers a critical examination of self psychology's theoretical concepts by someone who uses this framework extensively in his own work.

Robert D. Stolorow, Ph.D., is a Guest Faculty Member, Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute.

The development of this paper benefited enormously from numerous discussions with Dr. Bernard Brandchaft.

Some Notes on Hartmann's Ego Psychology and the Psychology of the Self

William Meissner S.J.

William Meissner

129 Mount Auburn Street
Cambridge, MA 01238

William Meissner  

The present contribution is an extension of previous efforts to bring into focus a more comprehensive psychology of the self that can be meaningfully articulated with existing psychoanalytic metapsychology (Meissner, 1981a, 1981b, 1983, 1986). Previous contributions have focused on the clinical phenomenology of the self (Meissner, 1981), and on the potential conceptual integration of a self concept within the structural theory (Meissner, 1983, 1986).

The term self psychology has been taken captive by the adherents to the views of Heinz Kohut (1966, 1977). I have argued elsewhere (Meissner, 1981) that the resulting psychology of the self is largely embedded in and interpreted in terms of narcissistic dynamics, and that such an approach to the psychology of the self is excessively restrictive and narrow. In my view, a psychology of the self involves more than merely the vicissitudes of narcissism; a more amplified view of the self, which embraces structural and instinctual vicissitudes beyond the confines of narcissism, offers much greater promise for a theoretical development that can more usefully be integrated with existing psychoanalytic views.

Dr. Meissner is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School.

Heinz Hartmann and Drive Theory: A Reevaluation

Jay Greenberg PHD

Jay Greenberg

275 Central Park West, 1B
New York, NY 10024

Jay Greenberg  

It is a measure of Heinz Hartmann's thinking that attempting to assess his contribution two decades after his death quickly leads to thoughts about the general state of psychoanalysis today. One cannot speak of Hartmann's contribution just to theory, or just to clinical practice, or just to the relationships between psychoanalysis and adjacent discipliness. He addressed all of these issues in condensed, interrelated ways — in many cases setting the terms for the debates that still occupy us as analytic thinkers and practitioners. Contemporary analysts operate far beyond the borders within which Freud created his new discipline. We see more and different sorts of patients, we have evolved new and more ambitious treatment goals, and we apply psychoanalytic principles in an expanding range of research settings. Probably none of this would have happened, or would have happened in quite the same way, without Hartmann's work.

Since Breuer first met Anna O. it has been fashionable to say that psychoanalysis is going through a particularly exciting and/or trying phase of its development. Usually, perhaps always, this has been true. But there is reason to think it even more true today. Until recently, adherents of a large number of competing theoretical models worked in isolation from each other.

Dr. Greenberg is on the Faculty and Supervisor of Psychotherapy, William Alanson White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis and Psychology.

Who Does Self Psychology Cure?

Christopher Bollas PHD

Christopher Bollas

Stockbridge, MA 01262

Christopher Bollas  

Sometime in the early 1960s Heinz Kohut lost his belief in the rhetoric of psychoanalysis. “I put theory on one side and practice on the other and, in my teaching, strained to talk about ego psychology as if it were in harmony with what I did in practice.” He knew that “psychoanalysis needed a decisive shift in emphasis, in both theory and practice” (1984, p. 87) but for several years he avoided this insight by devoting himself to “administrative work.”

His discontent with the theory of ego psychology was shared by many analysts during this period, who reconsidered the theory of drives and the nature of the ego. Within the American tradition, Roy Schafer, for example, emerged with a new philosophy of psychoanalytic rhetoric.

But Kohut was troubled by something else, and this becomes strikingly clear in How Does Analysis Cure? Psychoanalysts have become “stepped in a morality-tinged theory about the therapeutic centrality of truth-facing that is interwoven with a comparably morality-tinged scientific model about the need to make the unconscious conscious. In terms of this model, anything that opposes ‘making conscious’ or ‘becoming conscious’ is a resistance” (p. 141). He reflects on how he would now handle a specific clinical encounter differently: the patient who tells a lie.

Christopher Bollas, Ph.D., is a Member of the British Psycho-Analytic Society; Member, British Association of Psychotherapists; Visiting Professor of Psychoanalysis, University of Rome; Visiting Professor of English, University of Massachusetts; and Director of Education, Austen Riggs Center.

The Nuclear Threat: Its Impact on Psychoanalytic Conceptualizations

Martin Wangh MD

Martin Wangh

1 Diskin Street
92473 Jerusalem, Israel

Martin Wangh  

In the last room of the lowest floor of the Prado, in Madrid, in what almost constitutes an underground shelter, hangs an ominous painting by Francisco Goya y Lucientes. Two giants are swinging enormous clubs at each other while they seem to be sinking more and more deeply into the mire in which they stand. The entire scene is velied by fog. A prophetic representation, indeed, of our present world situation: The two superpowers threatening to engage in a war that may well bring about the end of the human species — and of much of the present biosphere in a blanketing nuclear winter.

What is the human, psychic reaction to such a threat? What effect does this menace have on the differentiations of the mind postulated by psychoanalysis? The experience of the Nazi Holocaust has given us a foretaste of the answers to these questions.

Hillel Klein (1983, p. 123), who was himself a survivor of the Nazi camps, wrote about the loss of differentiation in psychic structure during life in the camps. “Intrapsychic conflicts … were … characteristically diminished in the face of real danger … [under] the pressure of having to answer existential questions with life or death consequences for self and family.

Dr. Wangh is Training Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Emeritus, Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University, New York; and currently lives in Jerusalem where he is on the faculty of the Israel Psychoanalytic Society and Institute and Visiting Scholar at the Freud Center of the Hebrew University.

Male Sexuality and Power

Ethel Person MD

Ethel Person

135 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10023

Ethel Person  

Male psychology is beginning to attract the kind of attention paid to its female counterpart over the past 15 years. However, while the assumption that female sexual masochism is primary, universal, and defining has been challenged, the popular belief that male sexuality is innately aggressive and sadistic has persisted with minimal questioning.

The cultural stereotype of male sexuality is of a kind of phallic omnipotence and supremacy, a phallus invested with the power of mastery. At the very least, this macho view depicts a large, powerful, untiring phallus attached to a very cool male, long on self-control, experienced, competent, and knowledgeable enough to make women crazy with desire. As Zilbergeld has said “It's two feet long, hard as steel, and can go all night” (1978, p. 23). In the shared cultural fantasy, even the normally reticent female is perceived to be utterly powerless and receptive when confronted by pure macho sexuality.

But phallic power is also viewed as easily corrupted into sexual domination and violence. This is clear in the common depiction of male sexuality in pornography, movies, TV, and sexual humor, and in much of the major fiction of our time.

Ethel S. Person, M.D., is Director and Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research; Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University, College of Physicians and Surgeons. Earlier versions of this paper were presented at the William Alanson White Institute, September 19, 1984 and as “The Foundation Lecture” for the New Jersey Psychoanalytic Society, November 15, 1984. I thank Drs. Robert Michels and Arnold Rothstein, who read an earlier version of this paper and made extremely cogent suggestions.

Nuclear Conflict and the Nuclear Self

Theodore Shapiro MD

Theodore Shapiro

525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Shapiro  

How does analysis cure?, Kohut's last book prior to his death, provides us with a view of its author as a concerned clinician. This book leaves no doubt that Kohut's primary interest and emphasis during his later years was in the appropriate management of special clinical situations. This focus led him to recommendations for treatment that he insisted required revisions in clinical theory — even as Freud rewrote clinical theory during the evolution of his ideas. But in Kohut's revisions the theoretical adjustments that were recommended have come into sharp conflict with the classical psychoanalytic model, which was and is in common use. Some of Freud's various revisions we know so well: his theory of narcissism (1914), the structural theory (1923), the dual instinct theory (1920), and the theory of anxiety (1926), all blossomed in settings of controversy with colleagues. However, Freud was not only a respondent but the Urquell of our science. Moreover, he never quite gave up some of the principles and ideas that were the essentials of his early models. Thus, even late in life, Freud (1926) spoke of the possibility of real trauma, the importance of topography as a complement to structural theory in depth psychology, and actual anxiety — all despite the growing interest in ego psychology.

Dr. Shapiro is Editor of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association and Professor of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College.

But each honest thinker who is basically an empiricist has to have some truth in his position, no matter how extremely he has formulated it. The problem is to find the truth underneath the exaggeration, to cut away the excess elaboration or distortion and include the truth where it fits.

There is a sizeable core of truth in Kohut's theory of the therapeutic action of psychoanalysis, but it is a truth that is exaggerated and single-minded, and, moreover, one needs to know where it fits within preexisitng psychoanalytic knowledge.

Kohut compares the theories of self psychology to Brunelleschi's discovery of the laws of perspective, a discovery that transformed painting and taught men to see in a new way. Only time will tell whether self psychology has revolutionized our psychoanalytic vision, but if I may be permitted another visual analogy — self psychology is a high-power lens that may allow us to see things in greater detail, but at the expense of a significant narrowing of the visual field.

How does analysis cure? is a fitting capstone to Heinz Kohut's life's work. Here we have before us the considered conclusions of a psychoanalytic investigator who, as all who knew him can attest, was very careful to avoid premature closure, preferring to leave himself open to clinical experience as long as possible. In this volume (1984) he answers many of the questions that were raised over the years by both students and critics of self psychology, as his contributions to psychoanalysis have come to be called. Elizabeth Kohut writes in the preface that her husband told her that with this book he felt he had completed what he had hoped to accomplish, and indeed his sense of secure achievement and hard-earned conviction comes through clearly and convincingly in these pages. Although this posthumously published volume was prepared from a draft completed shortly before the author's death, the voice throughout is unmistakably Kohut's, there are no false notes, for this we are indebted to Arnold Goldberg, the book's editor, and his collaborator, Paul Stepansky.

Not surprisingly, no more than any of Kohut's other works, is this an easy book to read; it must, and deserves to be, studied carefully — the effort to do so will be amply rewarded.

Although the problem of power in mental life and human interaction has an important place in many psychosocial models, it has remained the stepchild of psychoanalysis. The phenomenology and explanatory value of power is too important to remain tangential and ambiguous within psychoanalysis. To find a significant place for the concept of power in psychoanalytic theory has been difficult since power implies a holistic and interactional viewpoint. These viewpoints cannot be easily reconciled with either a drive conflict or a deficit model.

We envision this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry as a pioneering effort, a beginning examination of the dimensions of power in psychoanalytic thought. We invited five contributors to address the problem of power. The result is a heterogeneous group of papers varying from studies of powerful historical figures to a reformulation of metapsychology.

In “Male Sexuality and Power,” Ethel Person proposes a new perspective on male power and sexuality. She takes issue with the view that aggression, phallic sadism, and castration anxiety are fundamental to male sexual fantasies and conflicts. She argues that a decisive role in male power also centers on narcissistic issues such as the fear of powerlessness in the control of the penis and the fear of loss of the love object.

Peter Loewenberg, in “Nixon, Hitler, and Power,” applies an ego psychology approach to the careers of two powerful politicians to suggest the variety and richness of psychoanalytic formulations that are now available to the psychohistorian.

What is the most powerful impulse of human beings in the face of night, of danger, of the unknown?—It is to run away; to avert the eyes and flee; to pretend the menace is not loping towards them in seven league boots. Vamik Volkan  

Any negotiations between opposing nations, according to Harold Saunders (1985), occurs in two phases. The first, largely political, is designed to help build political foundations, gain support for leadership, and remove obstacles to the resolution of international problems. The second is chiefly diplomatic and involves actual official negotiations. Davidson and Montville (1980-1981) refer to the preliminary, unofficial dialogues as Track II diplomacy, in order to distinguish them from official negotiations — Track I diplomacy. Some makers of foreign policy view Track II diplomatic talks as “confidence building” or “foundation building.”

During the past 15 years I have been present at many unofficial dialogues engaged in by representatives of national groups in conflict. As a member—and later as chairman—of the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the American Psychiatric Association, I attended a series of major and minor meetings between Egyptians and Israelis between 1980 and 1984. Throughout this period and earlier, I also participated in a number of semi-academic and semipolitical meetings of Turkish and Greek representatives in Cyprus.

Dr. Volkan is Professor of Psychiatry and Director of the Division of Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Virginia Medical School; he is also Medical Director, Blue Ridge Hospital, University of Virginia Medical Center, Charlottesville, Virginia.
